title: Reactions of Acids with Metal Oxides
content:
# Reactions of Acids with Metal Oxides

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Write equations for reactions between acids and metal oxides
- Describe observations for these reactions
- Explain why these are neutralisation reactions
- Use these reactions to make salts

## Introduction

Metal oxides are **bases** - they neutralise acids. When a metal oxide reacts with an acid, a salt and water are produced. This is a key method for preparing salts in the laboratory.

## Key Concepts

### General Equation

$$\text{Metal oxide} + \text{Acid} \rightarrow \text{Salt} + \text{Water}$$

This IS a neutralisation reaction (water is formed).

### Examples

**With hydrochloric acid (→ chloride salts):**
$$\text{CuO} + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{CuCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{MgO} + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{ZnO} + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{ZnCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**With sulfuric acid (→ sulfate salts):**
$$\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CuSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{MgO} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{ZnO} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**With nitric acid (→ nitrate salts):**
$$\text{CuO} + \text{2HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3\text{)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

### Why Are These Neutralisation Reactions?

- Metal oxides contain O²⁻ ions
- O²⁻ acts as a base, accepting H⁺ ions
- O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O
- The acid is neutralised
- Water is formed

### Common Metal Oxides

| Metal oxide | Colour | Salt colour (in solution) |
|-------------|--------|---------------------------|
| Copper(II) oxide (CuO) | Black | Blue |
| Magnesium oxide (MgO) | White | Colourless |
| Zinc oxide (ZnO) | White | Colourless |
| Iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) | Red-brown | Yellow/brown |
| Lead(II) oxide (PbO) | Yellow | Colourless |

### Observations

**Copper oxide + dilute sulfuric acid:**

[DIAGRAM: Black powder (CuO) being added to acid, forming blue solution (CuSO₄)]

**Observations:**
1. Black copper oxide powder is added to warm acid
2. The black solid gradually disappears
3. The solution turns blue (copper sulfate solution)
4. When excess oxide is added, some black solid remains
5. The mixture warms up (exothermic)

### Using This Reaction to Make Salts

**Method:**
1. Warm the acid gently in a beaker
2. Add metal oxide a little at a time, stirring
3. Continue until oxide stops dissolving (excess remains)
4. Filter to remove excess oxide
5. Evaporate the filtrate to crystallise the salt

**Why add excess oxide?**
- To ensure all the acid has reacted
- Unreacted oxide can be easily filtered off
- Ensures the salt solution is not contaminated with acid

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Write the equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid. Include state symbols.

**Solution:**
$$\text{ZnO(s)} + \text{2HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \text{ZnCl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

---

**Example 2:** Describe what you would observe when black copper oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid.

**Solution:**
- The black solid (copper oxide) dissolves/disappears
- The colourless solution turns blue
- The mixture warms up (reaction is exothermic)
- Effervescence is NOT observed (no gas is produced)

---

**Example 3:** Explain why the reaction of a metal oxide with an acid is called neutralisation.

**Solution:**
- Metal oxides are bases
- They can accept H⁺ ions from the acid
- The oxide ion (O²⁻) reacts with H⁺: O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O
- Water is formed
- The H⁺ ions are removed (acid is neutralised)
- Products are salt + water (typical of neutralisation)

---

**Example 4:** A student wants to make pure magnesium sulfate crystals from magnesium oxide and sulfuric acid. Describe the method.

**Solution:**
1. Pour dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker and warm gently
2. Add magnesium oxide powder, stirring continuously
3. Keep adding oxide until no more dissolves (excess remains)
4. Filter the mixture to remove excess magnesium oxide
5. Pour the filtrate (magnesium sulfate solution) into an evaporating basin
6. Heat gently to evaporate some water
7. Leave to cool and crystallise
8. Filter to collect crystals and dry with filter paper

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Expecting bubbles when metal oxide reacts with acid
- **Correct:** No gas is produced - this is NOT the metal + acid reaction

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that metal oxides are bases
- **Correct:** Metal oxides ARE bases (they neutralise acids)

- **Mistake:** Writing Fe₂O₃ + HCl → FeCl₃
- **Correct:** Need to balance properly: Fe₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2FeCl₃ + 3H₂O

## Practice Questions

1. Write the general word equation for the reaction of a metal oxide with an acid. (1 mark)

2. Write balanced equations for:
   a) Copper oxide + hydrochloric acid (2 marks)
   b) Magnesium oxide + sulfuric acid (2 marks)
   c) Iron(III) oxide + hydrochloric acid (2 marks)

3. Describe what you would observe when magnesium oxide powder is added to warm dilute hydrochloric acid. (3 marks)

4. Explain why adding copper oxide to sulfuric acid is a neutralisation reaction. (3 marks)

5. Describe how you would prepare a pure dry sample of zinc sulfate starting from zinc oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. (6 marks)

6. Why is excess metal oxide added when preparing a salt by this method? (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Metal oxide | A compound of a metal with oxygen; acts as a base |
| Base | A substance that neutralises an acid |
| Filtrate | The liquid that passes through a filter |
| Excess | More than enough to react with all of another substance |

## Summary

- **Metal oxide + Acid → Salt + Water**
- This is a **neutralisation** reaction
- Metal oxides are **bases**
- No gas is produced (unlike metal + acid)
- Observations: solid dissolves, solution may change colour, warms up
- **Method to make salts:**
  1. Add excess oxide to warm acid
  2. Filter off excess
  3. Evaporate and crystallise
- Colour changes help identify the reaction (e.g., black CuO → blue CuSO₄)
